strengths: First rigorous demonstration of early directional convergence for deep (L-homogeneous with L>2) neural networks with small initializations, extending a line of work previously restricted to two-homogeneous networks.

The key technical device (rescaling time by δ^{L-2}) is well-motivated and clearly explained; the paper also honestly identifies and handles a genuinely new technical difficulty, namely that the gradient flow of the NCF can blow up in finite time when L>2 (Lemma 5.2 vs. Lemma D.1), which requires a more careful analysis than the L=2 case.
The proofs in the appendices are complete and reasonably careful, using appropriate tools (unbounded KL inequality on o-minimal structures, Gronwall's inequality, homogeneity identities).

Limitations are discussed candidly: the locally Lipschitz gradient assumption excludes ReLU, the separable-structure assumption of Theorem 5.3 excludes fully connected deep networks, and the paper outlines the obstacles to removing these restrictions rather than overclaiming.

Supporting experiments on toy squared-ReLU and ReLU networks corroborate the theory and additionally reveal an unexplained low-rank structure in the weights, which is an interesting empirical observation connected to prior work.
weaknesses: The main theorem excludes ReLU networks (the most practically relevant activation) because gradients are required to be locally Lipschitz; the paper only provides informal empirical evidence and a discussion of why the proof breaks for ReLU.

Theorem 5.3 requires a separable weight structure H(x;w) = H_n + H_z, which by the authors' own admission excludes fully connected deep networks, substantially limiting the reach of the saddle-point result.

The results are purely qualitative: the constants T_ε, B_ε, δ̄ are implicit and can be extremely extreme as ε shrinks (the paper itself notes B_ε grows as ε decreases), and no convergence rates or effective bounds are given, making it hard to judge how 'early' the early phase is in practice.

Directional convergence is only to a non-negative KKT point of the constrained NCF, not necessarily a maximum or a canonical direction, which is a comparatively weak characterization of what the weights align to.

The contribution, while technically non-trivial, is incremental relative to Kumar & Haupt [1]; the conceptual novelty is essentially one rescaling step, and the empirical section is limited to small synthetic toy problems with no comparison to any downstream task or larger setting.

Some proof details rely on delicate estimates (e.g., the Taylor approximation bounds for the logistic loss in eq. (52), and the contradiction arguments around T̄_δ = T_ε) that would benefit from more explicit justification; a careful reader cannot easily verify all inequalities at a glance.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior rigorous results on early directional convergence under small initialization were restricted to two-layer or two-homogeneous networks, and this work provides what appears to be the first rigorous extension to L-homogeneous networks with L > 2.

The main technical device—rescaling time by δ^{L−2} and analyzing s(t) = w(t/δ^{L−2})/δ—is well motivated and clearly explained (Section 5.1.1), with the intuition that gradients scale as δ^{L−1} under L-homogeneity made explicit.

The proofs in the appendix (Lemma 5.2, Theorem 5.1, Theorem 5.3) are reasonably careful, using standard but appropriately combined tools: Gronwall's inequality, homogeneity identities (Euler's theorem), the unbounded Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality for definable functions from [31], and a finite-curve-length argument adapted from Ji & Telgarsky.

The authors honestly identify the boundaries of their results: they explicitly discuss why the technique does not extend to ReLU networks (Section 5.1.3), why Theorem 5.3 excludes fully connected deep networks, and they clearly state that the observed low-rank structure is not explained by their theory.
The toy experiments (Figures 1–5) are consistent with the theory and provide supporting empirical evidence, including for ReLU networks where the theory does not apply.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to [1] (Kumar & Haupt, 2024). The core proof architecture—comparing the rescaled dynamics against NCF gradient flow, plus the directional-convergence argument via Łojasiewicz and curve length—is inherited from that work. The genuinely new ingredients are the δ^{L−2} time rescaling and the handling of possibly unbounded NCF dynamics (Lemma 5.2, Lemma D.1), which, while non-trivial, do not constitute a broad conceptual advance.

The assumptions substantially limit practical relevance. Requiring locally Lipschitz gradients excludes ReLU networks—the architecture of primary practical interest—so the results apply mainly to linear, polynomial, and higher-power ReLU networks. Since the paper is motivated by understanding deep network training, and the empirical section itself demonstrates the phenomenon for ReLU networks that the theory cannot cover, the theory–practice gap is significant.

Theorem 5.3 (saddle points) requires a separable structure H = H_n + H_z, which the authors acknowledge excludes fully connected deep networks. Combined with Assumption 2 (including the technical stability condition (15)), the theorem covers a fairly narrow class of scenarios whose connection to saddle points actually encountered in training deep networks is not established.

The analysis is restricted to gradient flow. No discrete-time (gradient descent) results are given, and no justification is provided that the flow results are robust to discretization; given the long time scales T_ε/δ^{L−2} involved, this is a non-trivial omission.

The main theorem is a disjunctive statement: weights converge to a KKT point of the constrained NCF OR collapse to approximately 0. The paper does not characterize which branch occurs beyond noting it depends on w_0, weakening the predictive content of the result.

The quantitative constants are weak: the threshold δ̄ depends on ε, T_ε, and exponentially on K_ε‖y‖₂ (Eq. 45), and T_ε is defined only implicitly via convergence of the NCF flow. The result is essentially qualitative; nothing is said about how small δ must be relative to realistic initialization scales.

The empirical section is limited to small synthetic toy problems (100 points on a sphere in R^10, small random teacher networks) with a single random seed and no baselines or ablations; these illustrate but do not stress-test the theory (e.g., no verification of the δ^{L−2} time scaling across initialization scales).

strengths: First rigorous theoretical treatment of early directional convergence for deep (L>2) homogeneous neural networks with small initialization, extending prior work that was restricted to two-homogeneous networks.

The proofs are self-contained and careful, combining tools such as Gronwall's inequality, the unbounded Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality for definable functions, and Euler's homogeneity relations; the key technical innovation (time rescaling by δ^{L-2}) is clearly explained and well-motivated (Section 5.1.1).

The paper is transparent about its limitations: it explicitly discusses why ReLU networks are excluded (Section 5.1.3), why Theorem 5.3 applies only to separably structured networks (Section 5.2), and frames these as open problems rather than overclaiming.

Empirical illustrations (Figures 1-5) are consistent with the theory and honestly presented as motivation/illustration, including the observation of low-rank structure that the theory does not explain, which is flagged as future work.

The two-outcome characterization (directional convergence to a non-negative KKT point of the constrained NCF vs. approximate convergence to 0) is crisp, and the role of w0 and η in determining the outcome is clearly delineated.
weaknesses: The contribution is a fairly incremental extension of [1] (Kumar and Haupt, 2024): the overall proof architecture, the NCF framework, the KKT-point characterization, and even the saddle-point analysis closely follow [1]. The main novelty is the δ^{L-2} time rescaling and handling the possible finite-time blow-up of the NCF gradient flow (Lemma 5.2), which, while nontrivial, may not be sufficient for a top-tier contribution on its own.

The assumption of locally Lipschitz gradients excludes ReLU networks, arguably the most practically relevant class. The paper only offers empirical evidence and a differential-inclusion discussion of why the extension is hard, leaving the central practical case unresolved.

Theorem 5.3 (saddle points) applies only to networks with a separable output structure, which excludes fully connected deep neural networks; this substantially limits the reach of the second main result.
All results are for gradient flow, not gradient descent, and for noiseless/square or logistic losses on a fixed dataset; the gap to practical stochastic training is not addressed.

Experiments are small-scale toy examples (synthetic data on the unit sphere, small fixed networks, single runs, no code or experimental details sufficient for full reproducibility such as seeds or hyperparameter sensitivity); they serve as illustration rather than validation.

Some claims of being 'the first step' or 'no prior work that rigorously demonstrates early directional convergence for deeper networks' should be tempered given the closely concurrent [1] and related empirical works ([29], [30]) on deeper networks.

strengths: Extends the early directional convergence theory for small initializations from two-homogeneous networks (Kumar & Haupt, 2024) to deep L-homogeneous networks with L > 2, which is the first rigorous result of this kind for deep networks; previous rigorous work was limited to shallow/two-homogeneous cases.

The main conceptual innovation (the time rescaling s(t) = (1/δ) w(t/δ^{L-2})) is well motivated and clearly explained, and the proof handles genuinely new technical difficulties: the NCF gradient flow can blow up in finite time for L > 2, and the authors establish the blow-up rate ||u(t)||_2 ≥ κ/(T*-t)^{1/(L-2)}, which has no analogue in the two-homogeneous case.

The proofs are complete, careful, and self-contained in the appendices, using appropriate tools (unbounded Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality of Ji & Telgarsky for definable functions, Gronwall's inequality, Clarke subdifferential calculus for non-smooth activations in the KKT characterization part).

The second contribution (Theorems 3 and 4) gives clean, interpretable necessary and sufficient conditions for rank-one KKT points of the constrained NCF for Leaky ReLU and polynomial Leaky ReLU networks of arbitrary depth and arbitrary training data, together with a constructive reduction to a smaller optimization problem, and empirical validation (Tables 1-2) that the required rank-one and non-negativity assumptions hold for gradient-ascent solutions.

The paper is honest about limitations: it clearly states that Theorem 1 excludes deep ReLU networks (locally Lipschitz gradient assumption), devotes Appendix D to explaining exactly why the extension is hard, and the discussion of the two possible scenarios (KKT point vs. convergence to zero) is transparent.
Code is submitted with the paper, and experimental details (data generation, algorithm, initialization, stopping criterion, handling of non-differentiable activations) are adequately documented.
weaknesses: The main theorem covers only gradient flow with arbitrarily small initialization and requires locally Lipschitz gradients, which excludes deep ReLU networks — arguably the setting of greatest practical interest. The covered class (deep linear, polynomial ReLU, monomials) is somewhat specialized, and the extension to ReLU is explicitly left open.

The main result is a fairly natural generalization of Kumar & Haupt (2024, Theorem 5.1); the incremental technical novelty is essentially the δ^{L-2} time rescaling plus the finite-time blow-up analysis, which limits the depth of the conceptual advance.

The KKT-point characterization in Section 5 is conditional: the necessary conditions hold only under rank-one hidden-weight and (for α ≠ 1) non-negativity assumptions that are validated empirically on small synthetic instances (30 random instances, 2-3 layer networks, n=100) rather than proved. The important motivating question — why gradient descent converges to low-rank KKT points during early training — is left open, so the connection between the theory and the observed rank-one structure remains largely empirical.

The experimental validation is limited in scope: small networks, random data, no evidence on real datasets or on whether the empirical phenomena persist at scale, and the claim that gradient ascent 'seems to avoid' non-low-rank KKT points is not analyzed.

No results connect the early-stage behavior back to later training dynamics (e.g., loss decrease or generalization); the theorem's second scenario (weights approximately converging to zero) is not characterized in terms of w0, leaving the result partly descriptive.

strengths: The main theorem (Theorem 1) extends early directional convergence from two-homogeneous networks (Kumar & Haupt, 2024) to deep L-homogeneous networks with L > 2, filling a genuine gap since prior rigorous results were limited to shallow or two-homogeneous networks.

The proofs appear technically complete and careful: the appendix includes a full proof of the directional convergence of the NCF gradient flow (Lemma 2), handling the new difficulty that for L > 2 the NCF flow can blow up in finite time, with an explicit growth rate (eq. 29).
The time-rescaling idea s(t) = (1/δ)w(t/δ^{L-2}) is clean, well-motivated (the δ^{L-1} scaling of the gradient at initialization is clearly explained), and conceptually transparent.

The paper is honest about its limitations: it explicitly states that locally Lipschitz gradients exclude deep ReLU networks, devotes Appendix D to explaining why the extension is difficult, and acknowledges in the conclusion that the low-rank KKT convergence phenomenon remains unexplained.
The empirical validation of the rank-one and non-negativity assumptions (Tables 1 and 2) is a reasonable sanity check, and code is submitted alongside the paper, aiding reproducibility.

The KKT characterization (Theorems 3 and 4) is non-trivial, handling Clarke subdifferentials for non-smooth activations, and provides constructive sufficient conditions implying existence of rank-one KKT points for arbitrary data and depth.
weaknesses: The primary contribution is incremental. The core result (Theorem 1) is structurally a direct adaptation of Kumar & Haupt (2024, Theorem 5.1), with the main conceptual novelty being the time rescaling by δ^{L-2}; the paper itself concedes the phenomenon is 'similar to two-homogeneous networks... except for one difference.' The added value over the two-homogeneous case is modest.

The exclusion of ReLU networks significantly limits practical relevance. The assumption of locally Lipschitz gradients rules out the most practically important architecture, and the authors provide no fix, deferring this to future work. The theory thus applies mainly to deep linear, polynomial-ReLU, and monomial networks, whose training dynamics are of limited direct practical interest.

All results are for gradient flow with infinitesimally small steps; no guarantees or experiments connect the theory to discrete gradient descent, which is what practitioners use. The single toy experiment (a 10-20 neuron network on 100 synthetic points) is far too small to demonstrate empirical relevance at scale.

The second main contribution (Theorems 3 and 4) is conditional: it characterizes rank-one KKT points only under the rank-one and non-negativity assumptions, which are validated empirically on only 30 random instances of two- and three-layer networks. The paper does not establish that gradient ascent converges to such points, nor that such points are the ones relevant to training; this is explicitly left as an open question. As a result, the theorems risk characterizing a class of points whose connection to actual dynamics is unproven.

The necessity results require additional assumptions (α ≠ 1 plus non-negativity), so the 'necessary and sufficient' framing is only fully unconditional in special cases (α = 1); the abstract's phrasing slightly oversells this.

No comparison or contrast with other recently developed tools for small-initialization dynamics (e.g., incremental/stage-wise analyses such as Stöger & Soltanolkotabi, 2021; Abbe et al.-style leap analyses) is provided, making it hard to gauge whether the NCF-based approach offers advantages over alternatives.

strengths: The paper extends early directional convergence results from two-homogeneous networks (Kumar & Haupt, 2024) to genuinely deep L-homogeneous networks (L > 2), a regime where prior rigorous results were absent; this fills a real gap in the theory of small-initialization training dynamics.

The proof contains genuine technical novelty beyond a routine extension: the time rescaling by δ^{L−2} is a clean conceptual device, and the authors identify and handle the finite-time blow-up of the NCF gradient flow for L > 2 (Lemma 2), including a quantitative growth rate ∥u(t)∥₂ ≥ κ/(T*−t)^{1/(L−2)} that does not exist in the two-homogeneous case.

The characterization of rank-one KKT points of the constrained NCF (Theorems 3 and 4) for Leaky ReLU and polynomial activations is non-trivial, covers deep feed-forward networks with arbitrary data, and uses Clarke subdifferentials carefully to handle non-smooth activations.

The empirical work is well-matched to the theory: the authors explicitly quantify the rank-one and non-negativity assumptions via κ(·) and ρ(·) across random instances (Tables 1 and 2), rather than relying on qualitative claims, and the toy dynamics experiments (Figures 1–2) directly corroborate Theorem 1.

The presentation is generally clear: the proof sketch in Section 4.1.1 explains the rescaling intuition, and limitations are honestly discussed (exclusion of ReLU networks, challenges in Appendix D, non-convexity of the NCF meaning not all KKT points are low-rank).
weaknesses: The central assumption of locally Lipschitz gradients excludes deep ReLU networks, the practically most relevant architecture. The paper is candid about this (Appendix D), but it substantially limits the reach of the main theorem, and the polynomial activation class (max(x,αx)^p, p ≥ 2) is somewhat artificial.

The theorem is stated for gradient flow, not gradient descent, and characterizes the state only at the single rescaled time T̄ϵ with an approximation guarantee; it does not say what happens after, nor which KKT point is selected, so the 'convergence' picture is incomplete (acknowledged by the authors, but this narrows the contribution).

The two-outcome statement of Theorem 1 (converge to a non-negative KKT point or to approximately zero) leaves the second outcome largely unexplained and uninformative; the constant η and the scenario selection depend on w0 in an opaque way, so the theorem is existence-flavored rather than predictive.

The necessity results in Theorems 3–4 require the rank-one and non-negativity assumptions, which are only validated empirically on small random-data instances (30 instances, widths ≤ 3 layers, n = 100); there is no theoretical argument for why gradient ascent/descent avoids other KKT points, and the empirical validation is on toy problems.

The contribution is incremental relative to Kumar & Haupt (2024): the framework (NCF, KKT-point formulation, KL-inequality-based directional convergence argument) is inherited, and the novelty is the δ^{L−2} rescaling plus blow-up analysis. The KKT characterization part, while careful, is a self-contained optimization analysis somewhat loosely connected to the dynamics result (the connection 'GD converges to low-rank KKT points' remains empirical).

All experiments use tiny synthetic networks with random Gaussian labels; there is no experiment on structured data or on whether the identified KKT points are predictors of feature learning in any practically meaningful sense.
